questions.name: Transporting Cargo Safely
questions.text: After loading a flatbed and beginning a trip, the CDL manual gives a specific early-trip mileage at which the driver must inspect the cargo and securing devices. About how far into the trip is that first re-inspection required?

answers.text: Within the first 50 miles after beginning the trip
Within the first 5 miles after beginning the trip
Within the first 200 miles after beginning the trip
Only when crossing into another state

explanations.a: The CDL manual requires drivers to inspect the cargo and its securing devices within the first 50 miles after beginning a trip and make any adjustments needed.
explanations.b: Five miles is too short to detect settling or loosening of typical tiedowns under highway vibration.
explanations.c: 200 miles is well past the manual's required first re-inspection.
explanations.d: Re-inspection is keyed to mileage and time, not to state-line crossings.

questions.name: Transporting Cargo Safely
questions.text: Beyond the early-trip 50-mile check, the manual gives an ongoing rolling rule for re-inspecting cargo and securement during a long haul. Which standard matches the manual's rule?

answers.text: After every 1 hour or 50 miles of driving, whichever comes first
After every 3 hours or 150 miles of driving, whichever comes first
After every 6 hours or 400 miles of driving, whichever comes first
Only at fueling stops, regardless of duration

explanations.a: The manual's interval is longer than 1 hour or 50 miles for the rolling cargo check.
explanations.b: The manual instructs drivers to re-inspect cargo and securement after every 3 hours of driving or 150 miles, whichever comes first.
explanations.c: Six hours or 400 miles is well past the manual's stated interval.
explanations.d: Re-inspection is required on a time/mileage basis, not only at fueling stops.

questions.name: Transporting Cargo Safely
questions.text: The CDL manual lists a specific set of cargo-related responsibilities that fall on the driver regardless of who actually loaded the truck. Which set of four matches the manual's list?

answers.text: Sweeping the cargo deck, sealing all doors, weighing on a CAT scale, and photographing the load
Filing the bill of lading, billing the customer, dispatching, and submitting an electronic log
Inspecting cargo, recognizing overloads and poor balance, ensuring secure cargo that does not block the view, and ensuring access to emergency equipment
Refueling, washing the truck, replacing wiper blades, and verifying tire chains

explanations.a: Sweeping, sealing, scaling, and photographing are not the four-item responsibility list in the manual.
explanations.b: Paperwork and dispatching are administrative tasks, not the manual's four-item driver responsibility list.
explanations.c: The manual states the driver is responsible for inspecting cargo, recognizing overloads and poorly balanced weight, knowing the cargo is properly secured and does not obscure the view, and knowing the cargo does not restrict access to emergency equipment.
explanations.d: Vehicle maintenance items are not the four cargo responsibilities the manual identifies.

questions.name: Transporting Cargo Safely
questions.text: Even when mileage and time thresholds have not been reached, the CDL manual identifies one additional event that must trigger a cargo and securement re-inspection. Which event is it?

answers.text: After every refueling stop, regardless of how brief
After every meal stop of less than 15 minutes
Only when the trip-planning software prompts the driver
After every break the driver takes during driving

explanations.a: The manual ties re-inspection to driver breaks, not specifically to refueling stops.
explanations.b: The manual's trigger is any break, not specifically a meal stop under 15 minutes.
explanations.c: Trip-planning software is not the manual's stated trigger.
explanations.d: The CDL manual instructs drivers to re-inspect cargo and securing devices after every break taken during driving.

questions.name: Transporting Cargo Safely
questions.text: A driver picks up a sealed intermodal container and is told not to break the seal. According to the CDL manual, what cargo-related check still applies even though the driver cannot inspect the contents?

answers.text: Photographing each side of the container before departure
Verifying that the load does not exceed gross weight and axle weight limits
Removing the container's twist locks for safer transit
Counting the number of pallets visible through the doors

explanations.a: Photography is not a manual-mandated cargo check for sealed loads.
explanations.b: The manual states drivers cannot inspect sealed loads but should check that they do not exceed gross weight and axle weight limits.
explanations.c: Removing twist locks would unsecure the container and is the opposite of the manual's instruction.
explanations.d: Pallet counting is not the manual's required check; the requirement is on weight limits.

questions.name: Transporting Cargo Safely
questions.text: The CDL manual ties cargo inspection directly to a forward and lateral visibility requirement. Which statement matches the manual's requirement on cargo and the driver's view?

answers.text: The driver must know the cargo is properly secured and does not obscure the view ahead or to the sides
Cargo may obscure the side view as long as the rearview camera is operational
Cargo may obstruct forward visibility on closed-route private roads only
The driver must inspect the load only after the cargo has been positioned to block side mirrors

explanations.a: The manual states the driver must know the cargo is properly secured and does not obscure the view ahead or to the sides.
explanations.b: There is no rearview-camera carve-out in the manual; the requirement is on the actual view ahead and to the sides.
explanations.c: There is no private-road exception that allows cargo to block forward visibility.
explanations.d: Cargo that blocks side mirrors is exactly what the manual prohibits.

questions.name: Transporting Cargo Safely
questions.text: The CDL manual gives a precise definition of Gross Vehicle Weight Rating that drivers must understand to evaluate loading. Which definition matches the manual?

answers.text: The actual on-the-scale weight of a single vehicle on a given trip
The weight transmitted to the ground by one axle or set of axles
The value specified by the manufacturer as the loaded weight of a single vehicle
The maximum weight a tire can safely carry at a specified pressure

explanations.a: Actual scale weight is gross vehicle weight (GVW), not the manufacturer's rating.
explanations.b: That definition matches axle weight, not gross vehicle weight rating.
explanations.c: The CDL manual defines GVWR as the value specified by the manufacturer as the loaded weight of a single vehicle.
explanations.d: Maximum tire load at a specified pressure is the tire's rating, not GVWR.

questions.name: Transporting Cargo Safely
questions.text: For combination vehicles, the CDL manual defines Gross Combination Weight Rating with a specific construction. Which option matches the manual's definition?

answers.text: The value specified by the power-unit manufacturer if displayed on the FMVSS certification label, or the combined GVWR or GVW of the power unit and towed units producing the highest value
The actual loaded weight of all towed units only, excluding the power unit
The unladen curb weight of the tractor without trailer
The federal interstate maximum of 80,000 pounds, regardless of vehicle

explanations.a: The CDL manual defines GCWR as the value specified by the power-unit manufacturer on the FMVSS certification label, or the sum of GVWRs or GVWs of the power unit and towed units producing the highest value.
explanations.b: GCWR includes the power unit, not just the towed units.
explanations.c: Curb weight is unladen tractor weight, not the rated combination weight.
explanations.d: 80,000 pounds is the federal interstate maximum on most highways but it is not the definition of GCWR for any specific vehicle.

questions.name: Transporting Cargo Safely
questions.text: State maximum axle weights are often governed by a bridge formula tied to axle spacing. According to the CDL manual, what is the underlying purpose of the bridge formula?

answers.text: To equalize fuel taxes across all participating states
To set a single uniform axle limit independent of axle spacing
To allow more axle weight when axles are closer together
To permit less maximum axle weight for axles that are closer together, preventing overload of bridges and roadways

explanations.a: Bridge formulas govern weight, not fuel taxation.
explanations.b: The bridge formula is specifically about axle spacing; it does not set a uniform limit.
explanations.c: The relationship is the opposite: closer axles mean less allowed weight, not more.
explanations.d: The CDL manual states the bridge formula permits less maximum axle weight for axles that are closer together to prevent overloading bridges and roadways.

questions.name: Transporting Cargo Safely
questions.text: You are loading a flatbed with two large machines: one weighs 12,000 pounds and the other weighs 4,000 pounds. According to the CDL manual's center-of-gravity guidance, how should the heavier machine be positioned relative to the lighter one for safe handling?

answers.text: Place the heavier machine on top of the lighter one to keep weight concentrated near the cab
Place the heavier machine under the lighter one to keep the center of gravity as low as possible
Place both machines side by side at the very front of the trailer regardless of weight
Stack both machines as high as possible to minimize their footprint

explanations.a: Placing heavy cargo on top of light cargo raises the center of gravity, increasing rollover risk in curves.
explanations.b: The CDL manual instructs drivers to distribute cargo so it is as low as possible and to put the heaviest parts of the cargo under the lightest parts.
explanations.c: Concentrating both heavy and light cargo at the very front overloads the steering axle and creates handling problems.
explanations.d: High stacking creates a high center of gravity and is exactly what the manual warns against.

questions.name: Transporting Cargo Safely
questions.text: Concentrating too much weight over the steering axle of a tractor-trailer creates specific handling and equipment problems. According to the CDL manual, which problems are caused by excessive steering-axle weight?

answers.text: Drive wheels spin freely and lose traction in normal operation
The trailer rides too high and overhead clearances become inadequate
Steering becomes hard, and the steering axle and tires can be damaged
The vehicle becomes incapable of climbing any grade above 1 percent

explanations.a: Drive-wheel spin is associated with too little weight on the drive axles, not too much on the steering axle.
explanations.b: Overhead clearance is unrelated to steering-axle loading.
explanations.c: The CDL manual states that too much weight on the steering axle can cause hard steering and can damage the steering axle and tires.
explanations.d: Grade-climbing capability is not specifically tied to steering-axle overload in the manual.

questions.name: Transporting Cargo Safely
questions.text: On a refrigerated trailer, the freight is concentrated entirely at the rear nose, leaving the drive axles lightly loaded. The CDL manual warns this configuration creates a specific safety problem. Which problem does the manual identify?

answers.text: Poor traction at the drive wheels, which may spin easily, especially in bad weather
Excessive weight on the steering axle, causing very hard steering
Fully unloaded tires that cannot carry highway pressure
Automatic deactivation of the antilock braking system on slippery surfaces

explanations.a: The CDL manual states that too little weight on the driving axles can cause poor traction; the drive wheels may spin easily, and in bad weather the truck may not be able to keep going.
explanations.b: Hard steering is the problem caused by too much weight on the steering axle, not too little on the drive axles.
explanations.c: Tires retain their inflation pressure regardless of axle loading; underloading does not deflate tires.
explanations.d: ABS does not deactivate based on axle load distribution.

questions.name: Transporting Cargo Safely
questions.text: In cargo securement, the CDL manual describes blocking with a specific purpose and placement. Which option matches the manual's description of blocking?

answers.text: Securement that runs from the top of the cargo down to the deck or compartment walls
A federal stamp placed on the bill of lading to authorize sealing
A hand-tightened nylon strap of any rating crossing diagonally over the load
Material shaped to fit snugly against cargo and placed at the front, back, or sides to keep it from sliding

explanations.a: That description matches bracing, which runs from the top of the cargo to the deck or walls, not blocking.
explanations.b: Blocking is a physical securement device, not a paperwork stamp.
explanations.c: A loose nylon strap is a tiedown, and even then any rating is not adequate; it must meet working-load-limit rules.
explanations.d: The manual describes blocking as material shaped to fit snugly against cargo and placed at the front, back, or sides to keep cargo from sliding.

questions.name: Transporting Cargo Safely
questions.text: Federal cargo-securement regulations cited in the CDL manual set an aggregate working-load-limit rule for the tiedowns securing an article or group of articles. What does that rule require?

answers.text: The aggregate working load limit must equal twice the article's weight
The aggregate working load limit must be at least one-half the weight of the article or group of articles
The aggregate working load limit must equal the GVWR of the trailer
The aggregate working load limit must equal the article's weight in kilograms regardless of the unit system

explanations.a: Twice the article's weight is more conservative than the federal minimum; the rule requires at least one-half.
explanations.b: The CDL manual cites the federal rule that the aggregate working load limit of any securement system must be at least one-half the weight of the article or group of articles.
explanations.c: The trailer's GVWR is unrelated to the securement-system working-load-limit calculation.
explanations.d: The federal rule is based on the cargo weight, not on a metric-conversion artifact.

questions.name: Transporting Cargo Safely
questions.text: The CDL manual gives a length-based minimum count of tiedowns for cargo on a flatbed, plus an absolute floor for any load. Which combination matches the manual's rule?

answers.text: At least one tiedown for each 10 feet of cargo, with a minimum of two tiedowns regardless of how small the cargo is
At least one tiedown for each 25 feet of cargo, with no minimum count
At least three tiedowns for each 10 feet of cargo and at least four total
Tiedowns are not required as long as the load is in a closed van

explanations.a: The CDL manual states that cargo should have at least one tiedown for each 10 feet of cargo and that no matter how small the cargo, it must have at least two tiedowns.
explanations.b: The interval and minimum in this option do not match the manual's rule.
explanations.c: Three tiedowns per 10 feet exceeds the manual's stated minimum.
explanations.d: The manual notes that tiedowns can also be important in closed vans to prevent cargo shifting.

questions.name: Transporting Cargo Safely
questions.text: A driver loads a single 24-foot piece of structural steel on a flatbed. Applying the CDL manual's per-length tiedown rule, what is the minimum number of tiedowns required for this load?

answers.text: Exactly two tiedowns, the absolute floor for any cargo
Exactly two tiedowns, ignoring the per-length rule for steel
Three tiedowns, because 24 feet rounds up to three 10-foot increments and meets the minimum of two
Five tiedowns, one for each 5 feet of cargo length

explanations.a: The two-tiedown floor applies only when the per-length rule does not yield a higher count; here it does.
explanations.b: There is no exception that ignores the per-length rule for steel cargo; the per-length rule still applies.
explanations.c: Twenty-four feet of cargo requires at least one tiedown for each 10 feet, which rounds up to three; this also meets the minimum of two.
explanations.d: The manual's per-length rule uses 10-foot increments, not 5-foot increments.

questions.name: Transporting Cargo Safely
questions.text: The CDL manual identifies a specific structural feature on a flatbed or stake-bed truck that helps protect the driver from cargo shifting forward in a hard stop. What is this feature called and what is its purpose?

answers.text: A trailer skirt, used to reduce aerodynamic drag at highway speed
A front-end header board, often called a headache rack, that blocks forward movement of cargo and protects the driver in a crash or hard stop
An ICC bumper, used to protect cars that strike the rear of the trailer
A landing gear assembly, used to support a parked trailer

explanations.a: Trailer skirts are aerodynamic devices and have no securement function.
explanations.b: The CDL manual identifies the front-end header board, also called a headache rack, as a structure that blocks forward cargo movement and protects the driver in a crash or emergency stop.
explanations.c: The ICC bumper is a rear underride guard; it does not protect the cab from cargo shift.
explanations.d: Landing gear supports a parked trailer and has no role in cargo containment.

questions.name: Transporting Cargo Safely
questions.text: In cargo securement, the CDL manual distinguishes blocking from bracing by where each piece of material runs. Which description matches the manual's definition of bracing?

answers.text: Material attached to the front bumper of the tractor that supports the cab in a frontal impact
A nylon mesh laid across the top of cargo to keep small items from blowing off
Material that goes from the upper part of the cargo to the floor or walls of the cargo compartment
A spreader bar mounted on top of the trailer to discourage roof intrusion in a rollover

explanations.a: Bracing is internal cargo securement, not a tractor body feature.
explanations.b: Top netting helps with debris but is not the manual's definition of bracing.
explanations.c: The CDL manual defines bracing as material that goes from the upper part of the cargo to the floor or walls of the cargo compartment, used to prevent movement.
explanations.d: A spreader bar is unrelated to cargo bracing.

questions.name: Transporting Cargo Safely
questions.text: Dry bulk tank trailers carry loose loads such as flour, sand, or grain. According to the CDL manual, why do these loads call for extra caution on curves and turns?

answers.text: They produce excessive noise that may startle other drivers
They generate static electricity that interferes with the engine ECM
They have a high center of gravity, and the load can shift inside the tank
They cannot be re-inspected during a trip under federal rules

explanations.a: Noise is not the manual's stated handling concern for dry bulk.
explanations.b: Static-electricity issues with engine electronics are not the dry-bulk concern in the manual.
explanations.c: The CDL manual states dry bulk tanks have a high center of gravity and the load can shift, so drivers must be extremely cautious going around curves and making sharp turns.
explanations.d: There is no rule prohibiting in-trip re-inspection of dry bulk tanks.

questions.name: Transporting Cargo Safely
questions.text: Hanging meat in a refrigerated trailer creates a specific handling concern that the CDL manual highlights for ramp turns. What does the manual cite as the underlying issue?

answers.text: Hanging meat sets off airbag sensors at low speeds
Hanging meat is unstable with a high center of gravity, requiring special caution on sharp curves such as off ramps and on ramps
Hanging meat falls automatically below 32 degrees Fahrenheit and shifts mass forward
Hanging meat is exempt from re-inspection rules during a trip

explanations.a: There is no airbag-sensor interaction described in the manual.
explanations.b: The CDL manual states that hanging meat in a refrigerated truck is a very unstable load with a high center of gravity, and particular caution is needed on sharp curves such as off ramps and on ramps.
explanations.c: Hanging meat does not fall automatically with temperature, and there is no temperature-triggered shift described in the manual.
explanations.d: Hanging meat is not exempt from re-inspection rules.

questions.name: Transporting Cargo Safely
questions.text: Hauling livestock at less than full trailer capacity creates a known handling problem. According to the CDL manual, what loading practice does the manual recommend to manage this problem?

answers.text: Run the trailer empty rather than partially loaded
Add water tanks to the trailer to bring weight up to capacity
Set the parking brake at intersections to keep livestock from moving
Use false bulkheads to keep livestock bunched together

explanations.a: The manual does not require running empty; it instructs drivers to use false bulkheads with partial loads.
explanations.b: Adding water tanks to fill out the trailer is not the manual's recommended practice.
explanations.c: Setting the parking brake at intersections is unrelated to the livestock-shifting issue.
explanations.d: The CDL manual instructs drivers to use false bulkheads to keep livestock bunched together when carrying less than a full load, since livestock can lean on curves and shift the center of gravity.

questions.name: Transporting Cargo Safely
questions.text: Loads that exceed normal length, width, or weight limits are subject to special operating rules. According to the CDL manual, which condition typically applies to over-length, over-width, or overweight loads?

answers.text: They require special transit permits, often with driving limited to certain times
They are exempt from federal hours-of-service rules
They may be driven without warning signs as long as flashers are on
They may not be operated on any interstate highway under any condition

explanations.a: The CDL manual states over-length, over-width, or overweight loads require special transit permits, and driving is usually limited to certain times.
explanations.b: Oversized-load operations remain subject to federal hours-of-service rules; permits do not exempt drivers.
explanations.c: Special equipment such as wide-load signs, flashing lights, and flags is required, not just flashers.
explanations.d: Oversized loads can operate on interstates with the proper permit and equipment.

questions.name: Transporting Cargo Safely
questions.text: Drivers cover open-bed loads with tarps for two basic reasons identified in the CDL manual. Which pair of reasons matches the manual?

answers.text: To improve fuel economy and to reduce trailer noise
To shield the driver from cab glare and to reduce tire heat
To save on tiedown count and to lengthen vehicle inspection intervals
To protect people from spilled cargo and to protect the cargo from weather

explanations.a: Fuel economy is a side effect of some covers but is not the manual's listed reason.
explanations.b: Cab glare and tire heat are not the manual's stated reasons for covering cargo.
explanations.c: Cargo covers are unrelated to tiedown count or inspection intervals.
explanations.d: The CDL manual gives two basic reasons for covering cargo: to protect people from spilled cargo and to protect the cargo from weather.

questions.name: Transporting Cargo Safely
questions.text: Beyond permits and warning equipment, the CDL manual identifies an additional resource that may be required for some oversized loads on certain routes. What additional resource does the manual list?

answers.text: A second driver in the sleeper berth at all times
A continuous cell-phone connection to the dispatcher
A police escort or pilot vehicles bearing warning signs and flashing lights
A federal Department of Transportation inspector riding in the cab

explanations.a: The manual does not require a second driver for oversized loads.
explanations.b: Cell-phone connection is not a manual-mandated resource.
explanations.c: The CDL manual states such loads may require a police escort or pilot vehicles bearing warning signs and flashing lights.
explanations.d: DOT inspectors do not ride in cabs as a routine oversized-load resource.

questions.name: Transporting Cargo Safely
questions.text: Federal regulation 49 CFR 392.9, reflected in the CDL manual, places ultimate responsibility for cargo securement on a specific person, regardless of who actually loaded the truck. Who is that person?

answers.text: The driver, who must inspect cargo and ensure it is properly distributed and secured
The shipper, after the trailer doors close
The receiver, once the trailer arrives at the dock
The dispatcher, who creates the trip plan

explanations.a: 49 CFR 392.9 makes the driver responsible for ensuring cargo is properly distributed and secured, regardless of who loaded the truck.
explanations.b: The shipper has loading duties but the driver retains responsibility under 49 CFR 392.9.
explanations.c: The receiver has unloading duties; transit responsibility is the driver's.
explanations.d: The dispatcher does not bear the federal in-transit cargo responsibility.

questions.name: Transporting Cargo Safely
questions.text: The driver's cargo responsibilities under federal rules include ensuring the load does not block access to certain critical items in the cab. Which type of item must remain accessible?

answers.text: The driver's lunch box and personal phone charger
The trailer's electronic logging device only
The dispatcher's printed trip sheet only
Emergency equipment such as fire extinguisher, spare fuses, and warning devices

explanations.a: Personal items are not the focus of the federal access requirement.
explanations.b: The ELD is one item but the manual's focus is on emergency equipment more broadly.
explanations.c: Trip sheets are not the focus of the federal cargo-access requirement.
explanations.d: The CDL manual states the driver must know cargo does not restrict access to emergency equipment, including the fire extinguisher, spare fuses, and warning devices.

questions.name: Transporting Cargo Safely
questions.text: The CDL manual notes that legal maximum weights may not always be safe operating weights. Under which conditions does the manual specifically suggest a driver consider operating below the legal maximum?

answers.text: When a competing carrier has set lower internal weight standards
During bad weather or in mountains, where legal maximum weights may not be safe
On any route over 500 miles, regardless of conditions
Only when the dispatcher specifically requests it in writing

explanations.a: Competitor weight standards are not the basis for the manual's recommendation.
explanations.b: The CDL manual states that during bad weather or in mountains, it may not be safe to operate at legal maximum weights and instructs drivers to take that into account before driving.
explanations.c: The manual does not give a 500-mile threshold.
explanations.d: The decision to operate below legal maximums for safety is the driver's, not contingent on dispatcher requests.

questions.name: Transporting Cargo Safely
questions.text: Federal cargo rules establish minimum standards, but the CDL manual cautions that additional rules may apply on specific routes. What does the manual specifically warn drivers to know?

answers.text: Federal, state, and local regulations for commercial vehicle weight, securing cargo, covering loads, and where large vehicles can drive vary from place to place
State rules are preempted in all cases by federal cargo regulations
Local jurisdictions cannot regulate where commercial vehicles can drive
Cargo weight rules are uniform across all 50 states and require no local research

explanations.a: The CDL manual states that federal, state, and local regulations for commercial vehicle weight, securing cargo, covering loads, and where large vehicles can drive vary from place to place, and drivers must know the rules where they will be driving.
explanations.b: State rules are not preempted across the board; many areas allow stricter state requirements.
explanations.c: Local jurisdictions can and do regulate truck routes within their authority.
explanations.d: Weight rules are not uniform; they vary, especially with bridge formulas and route-specific limits.

questions.name: Transporting Cargo Safely
questions.text: A driver discovers their dispatched load requires hazardous-materials placards but the driver's CDL has no hazmat endorsement. According to the CDL manual, what is the consequence of driving the placarded load anyway?

answers.text: There is no consequence; placards are advisory only
Only the dispatcher faces a fine; the driver is shielded from liability
The driver may operate the load until the next scale, then turn back
It is a crime; when stopped, the driver will be cited and not allowed to drive the truck

explanations.a: The manual specifically calls placards mandatory for placard-required loads, not advisory.
explanations.b: The driver is not shielded from liability; both employer and driver face consequences.
explanations.c: There is no until-the-next-scale grace period in federal rules.
explanations.d: The CDL manual states driving a placarded vehicle without the hazardous materials endorsement is a crime, and when stopped, the driver will be cited and not allowed to continue driving the truck.

questions.name: Transporting Cargo Safely
questions.text: A dock crew at the shipper's facility loads and tarps a flatbed while the driver is in the dispatcher's office. The driver returns and is told to depart immediately. According to the CDL manual, what is the driver's cargo responsibility in this case?

answers.text: The driver bears no cargo responsibility because the shipper's crew loaded the truck
The driver may depart immediately, since the shipper's seal transfers responsibility
The driver remains responsible for inspecting cargo, recognizing overloads, and ensuring proper securement, regardless of who actually loaded the truck
The driver may rely on the dispatcher's verbal assurance that the load is properly secured

explanations.a: Federal cargo responsibility under 49 CFR 392.9 follows the driver, not the loader.
explanations.b: Sealing does not transfer cargo-securement responsibility under federal rules.
explanations.c: The CDL manual states that whether or not the driver loads and secures the cargo personally, the driver is responsible for inspecting cargo, recognizing overloads, and ensuring proper securement and access to emergency equipment.
explanations.d: Verbal assurance from a dispatcher does not satisfy the driver's federal cargo-inspection responsibility.
